title: Collapse at Station 7
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: Tuesday, 9:40 a.m., freestanding unit in Pasig. Mr. Arnel Gutierrez, 61, two hours into dialysis, collapses: unresponsive, not breathing, no pulse. The physician-on-duty stepped out to the pharmacy next door. You are the ACLS-current nurse leading until she returns. Compressions start within 15 seconds; pads go on at 40 seconds. The screen shows a chaotic trace.

n1.prompt: First rhythm check. What do you do?

choices.text: VF: “Charging, continue compressions. Everyone clear.” Shock, then compress.
choices.feedback: VF is shockable; shock early and resume compressions at once. “Everyone clear: patient, chair, lines, machine. Shock.” Compressions immediately.

choices.text: Wait for the physician-on-duty to come back before shocking, since only the physician decides on defibrillation.
choices.feedback: A trained nurse defibrillates per protocol; waiting lowers the chance of success with each minute.

choices.text: Give epinephrine first to make the heart more likely to respond, then shock at the next check.
choices.feedback: On the shockable path, the shock comes first; epinephrine follows failed initial shocks.

n2.scene: Second rhythm check: still VF. Second shock delivered; compressions resume.

choices.text: Epinephrine 1 mg IV through the secured venous needle, then every 3 to 5 minutes.
choices.feedback: After initial shocks fail, epinephrine 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes is reasonable (COR 2a). The circuit nurse confirms the needle; the recorder calls the time of the next dose.

choices.text: Give epinephrine at every two-minute rhythm check, so the drug always matches the CPR cycle.
choices.feedback: Every 2 minutes is too often; every other cycle keeps 3 to 5 minutes.

choices.text: Give 5 mg of epinephrine now to make up for the minutes lost before the pads went on.
choices.feedback: High-dose epinephrine is not recommended (COR 3: No Benefit).
choices.then: The drug nurse reads back and the leader corrects to 1 mg.

n3.scene: Third check: VF persists after three shocks and one epinephrine. The physician-on-duty returns.

choices.text: Summary, “You have the lead,” shock again, antiarrhythmic per protocol.
choices.feedback: Shock-refractory VF: amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered (COR 2b). A clean leadership handover keeps one voice. Give the 15-second summary; consider amiodarone 300 mg (or lidocaine) per protocol and review the causes aloud.

choices.text: Both of you give orders until it settles, so nothing is missed while the physician catches up.
choices.feedback: Two leaders cause duplicated and missed actions.
choices.then: The physician asks for a summary and takes the lead.

choices.text: Routine calcium and bicarbonate now, since every dialysis arrest should be treated as high potassium.
choices.feedback: Routine calcium and bicarbonate are not recommended; give them only for a specific cause per protocol.
choices.then: The physician asks for the last potassium first.

n4.scene: After the fourth shock and amiodarone, the rhythm check shows organized narrow complexes at 88.

choices.text: Feel for a definite pulse within 10 seconds.
choices.feedback: An organized rhythm needs a pulse check; the rhythm alone does not mean circulation. A pulse and a pressure mean ROSC; no pulse means PEA and compressions resume.

choices.text: Stop CPR: an organized rhythm is back on the monitor, so the heart is pumping again.
choices.feedback: Stopping without a pulse check risks leaving PEA untreated.
choices.then: A nurse feels for a pulse: present, pressure 92/58.

end.title: 10:05 a.m.
end.text: Mr. Gutierrez has ROSC and is handed over to the ambulance with the recorder’s sheet, a 12-lead ECG, and the dialysis facts.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Shock VF early; compress immediately after.
  • Epinephrine after the initial shocks fail, then every 3 to 5 minutes, 1 mg.
  • Refractory VF: amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered; no routine calcium or bicarbonate.
  • ROSC is a pulse and a pressure.
